sources.news_title: Georgia school shooter Colt Gray sentenced to life in prison without parole
sources.text:
Colt Gray, the Georgia teen who fatally shot two teachers and two students and wounded nine others at Apalachee High School in September 2024, was sentenced Tuesday to life in prison without the possibility of parole.
“Your crimes do reflect permanent incorrigibility and I will sentence you to life without parole for each of the malice murders you committed,” Judge Nicholas Primm said in announcing the sentence.
Colt, 16, did not appear to react to the sentence. He declined to speak to the court before the decision.
The families of the shooting victims and survivors gasped and audibly cried at the announcement in court.
The decision concludes a three-day sentencing hearing that has featured Colt’s guilty plea, emotional victim impact statements, his confessions to police and insights into his motive and mental health.
Barrow County District Attorney Brad Smith had asked the judge to sentence the teen to life without parole, saying he carried out the attack to be famous in a twisted online subculture that glorifies mass shooters.
“I know he’s had a bad upbringing, but … in this courtroom we’ve seen a lot worse,” Smith said. “And he’s the only one in the history of Georgia who has ever taken an assault rifle into a public school and opened fire on perfect strangers simply so he could be famous.”
Defense attorney Charlton Allen emphasized Colt’s young age and said he was “not irretrievably broken.” He asked for a sentence of life with the possibility of parole, saying life without parole is too harsh for any teenager.
The case stems from the attack at Apalachee High School in Winder, Georgia, on September 4, 2024, the deadliest school shooting in the state’s history.
That morning, school officials and resource officers had gone to intercept the then-14-year-old after he made several concerning comments. But in a stranger-than-fiction mix-up, they confused him with another student named Kolton Gray.
Colt then armed himself with an AR-15-style rifle — which he had brought to school hidden in his backpack — and fired indiscriminately into a math class before shooting several people in the hallway. Teachers Richard Aspinwall and Cristina Irimie and students Mason Schermerhorn and Christian Angulo were killed, and nine others were injured.
He surrendered to police that day and has remained behind bars since. He pleaded guilty Friday to 55 charges, including four counts of murder.
The US Supreme Court has ruled juveniles cannot be sentenced to death and can only be sentenced to life in prison without parole in rare circumstances. Judge Primm said he believed this was one of those cases.
Colin Gray, the teen’s father, was found guilty of murder and manslaughter charges in March for purchasing his son the rifle as a Christmas gift and leaving it unsecured in their house, despite warnings that Colt was a danger to others. He is scheduled to be sentenced Thursday.
This Friday, about five miles south of the Barrow County Courthouse, students will return to Apalachee High School for the first day of the new school year.
Parents investigated for neglect, abuse
Colin Gray’s trial earlier this year revealed the extent of Colt’s tumultuous childhood, and testimony Tuesday from his grandmother and a state official further detailed the family’s troubles.
His mother, Marcee Gray, struggled with drug and alcohol addiction, and the family moved repeatedly. School records show he was repeatedly absent from class, including missing his entire eighth-grade year. Family members spoke about Colt’s deteriorating mental health.
Colt’s grandmother, Deborah Polhamus, laid out a timeline of the family’s unsettled life, calling Marcee and Colin Gray “completely dysfunctional.” Colt had specific issues with his parents, she said.
“Colt was the one who seemed to have the most difficulty living with his dad and mother,” she said.
Polhamus said she believes Colt can be rehabilitated with proper mental health treatment.
“The Colt that I knew and the Colt that I know now is not the Colt that did all of this,” she said. “His mind was so distorted and … he had convinced himself that this was the way for him to go because then he could be somebody. All he ever wanted was to have a friend. All he ever wanted was to be included and loved.”
His parents had a “plethora of issues” related to child abuse and neglect, Candice Broce, the director of the Georgia Division of Family and Children Services, testified on Tuesday.
Last October, Colt was placed into emergency foster care because his mother was violating a court order limiting her contact with him, Broce said. His maternal grandmother, Deborah Polhamus, was named as his guardian.
The no-contact order against Marcee Gray, combined with the start of medication, had “changed him into essentially a different child,” Broce said. He began eating better, sleeping better and was more engaged with juvenile custody programming, she said.
Marcee Gray has not been accused of criminal wrongdoing in this case. Smith said she did not face charges because she did not have custody of Colt and did not possess the firearms at the time of the shooting.
Shooter’s motive was infamy
Colt Gray carried out the attack “to gain some sort of fame or notoriety from it,” Ashley Gilleland, an investigator with the Barrow County District Attorney’s Office, testified Tuesday.
“(I) wanna make history,” Colt wrote on the messaging platform Discord more than a year before the shooting. “I want people to remember the pain I caused and research me for hours.”
Colt’s journal writings and statements to police show he tried to copy and reference other mass shooters, particularly Nikolas Cruz, the Parkland school shooter. Gilleland said he put in coded “Easter egg” references to other mass shooters in his notebook and in his confessions.
“My love for Nik has formed into something in which I can find no other resort that can prove my love and affection towards him,” he wrote in a message days before the shooting.
After the shooting, he repeatedly asked his mother to search his name online and bring him “fan art” of himself, according to jail phone calls played in court.
“I’m in the big leagues, bro. And not in a bad way,” he said in one call.
Psychologist, investigators and victims spoke
Kevin Richards, a forensic psychologist, testified Monday that the teen’s paranoia, depression and anxiety were exacerbated by neglect and abuse at home and an online fixation with mass shooters.
But on cross-examination, Richards said Colt had exaggerated his mental health symptoms and made things up to try to get a more serious diagnosis. Colt did not show signs of mania, insanity, schizophrenia or bipolar disorder, Richards said, and there was no evidence he had hallucinations.
On Friday, the courtroom heard recordings of Colt’s interview with investigators less than an hour after the shooting. Sobbing and gasping, he apologized and offered paranoid, hallucinatory explanations for his actions, saying he believed teachers were plotting against him.
However, several of his statements were later proved false, including those about where he found the firearm and his claim that he called a suicide hotline before the attack. Barrow County Sheriff’s Office investigator Jason Smith said he believed Colt’s hysterical state was “performative.”
In victim impact statements Friday, family members and survivors stood before the court and described who they were before September 4, 2024, and who they have become since.
“I started to hate myself because I couldn’t truly live anymore, because I let you take every piece of joy I had away from me,” said Nautica Walton, who was in ninth grade when she was shot in the leg.
“I hate everything about you,” she told Colt. “I hate the scars you left on my body. I hate that you took innocent lives in front of innocent people. Most of all, I hate that I let you live in my mind.”
The families of the victims said they would never forget their lost loved ones.
“The defendant’s family will still get to see their son, talk to him and know he is breathing,” said Ismael Angulo Jr., the oldest sibling of victim Christian Angulo. “My mother (and) my father don’t get that privilege. The only way to visit Christian now is by standing over his grave.”
He added: “There is no fairness in that reality.”
CNN’s Andy Rose, Devon M. Sayers, Alaa Elassar, Sarah Hutter and Rebekah Riess contributed to this report.

Apalachee High School shooter Colt Gray gets life without parole
BARROW COUNTY, Ga. - Colt Gray, the 16-year-old accused of killing two students and two teachers in Apalachee High School in September 2024, was sentenced on Tuesday by a Barrow County Superior Court judge to life without parole after entering a non-negotiated plea.
Apalachee High School sentencing
What we know:
A Barrow County judge sentenced 16-year-old Colt Gray to life in prison without parole Tuesday after he pleaded guilty to 55 counts, for killing four people and injuring 11 others at Apalachee High School.
Barrow County Superior Court Judge Nicholas Primm sentenced 16-year-old Colt Gray to serve life in prison without the possibility of parole. Gray pleaded guilty on Friday to 55 counts, including murder, stemming from the Sept. 4, 2024, attack about 45 miles north-east of Atlanta.
A memorial for Cristina Irimie, Mason Schermerhorn, Richard Aspinwall and Christian Angulo in front of Apalachee High School in Winder on Sept. 11, 2024 (FOX 5)
The shooting claimed the lives of 14-year-old students Mason Schermerhorn and Christian Angulo, along with teachers Richard Aspinwall, 39, and Cristina Irimie, 53. Seven people sustained gunshot wounds, while four others were injured in the chaos, according to court testimony.
PREVIOUS STORY: What testimony revealed during day two of Colt Gray's sentencing
Courtroom testimony and ruling
What they're saying:
Judge Primm stated that while Gray was failed by his parents and family, those failures did not absolve him of who he chose to become. Primm ruled that Gray's actions reflected permanent incorrigibility rather than the transient immaturity of youth, noting Gray studied past trial transcripts and critiqued victim impact statements before acting.
Defense attorney W. Charlton Allen argued that Gray was not irretrievably broken and sought parole eligibility to offer hope. Gray's grandmother, Debbie Polhamus, testified that his parents failed him and that his behavior had improved significantly after receiving medication and treatment in detention.
Online mass shooter subculture
The backstory:
Investigators testified that Gray spent over a year planning the attack while deeply involved in an online group called the "true crime community". Gray stored over 2,000 photos of Parkland shooter Nikolas Cruz on his phone and carved the number 38 into his rifle.
During post-shooting jail phone calls, Gray excitedly asked his mother to look up fan art and social media commentary about him, prosecutors noted. District Attorney Brad Smith stated Gray placed deliberate "Easter eggs" on the day of the shooting to perpetuate his fame within the online subculture.
District attorney addresses parents
Why you should care:
District Attorney Brad Smith warned parents that online true crime groups lack political ideology and are driven purely by nihilism and a desire to cause pain. Smith urged families to monitor what their children post on social media or display in their bedrooms and immediately remove access to firearms if concerning signs appear.
Smith added that prosecutors did not charge Gray's mother because she lacked physical custody, lived in the county for only three months over two years, and did not supply the gun. Gray's father was tried separately after supplying the weapon, according to the district attorney.
Post-trial proceedings
What's next:
Official court records have not confirmed whether Gray will file a notice for a discretionary appeal within the 30-day post-sentencing window. Additionally, court officials have not indicated if Gray plans to submit a motion to withdraw his guilty plea.
Colin Gray, Colt's father, is expected to be sentenced on Thursday.
Prosecutors argued he ignored warning signs about his son's mental state.
It was the first time in state history a parent was convicted in connection with a school shooting carried out by their child.
Joshua Schiffer, an Atlanta-based attorney, said it made sense from a legal standpoint to wait for the father's sentencing.
"Colin Gray's crime is directly linked to what his son did, in a unique way that George has never really dealt with before," Schiffer said. "After the court obtained the conviction of Colin Gray, it was well within their discretion and arguably best practices to see what other facts evolved during the processing of Colt Gray's case."
The 55-year-old faces up to 180 years in prison on the 27 counts a jury convicted him on in March.

sources.news_title: Families of Apalachee school shooting victims want maximum sentence for Colt Gray
sources.text:
BARROW COUNTY, Ga. — A judge could decide on Monday the fate for the teen who pleaded guilty to the deadly Apalachee High School shooting.
Colt Gray changed his plea to guilty on Friday to all 55 charges for the Sept. 4, 2024 shooting. Four people died in the shooting: teachers Ricky Aspinwall and Cristina Irimie and students Mason Schermerhorn and Christian Angulo. Several others were injured.
A psychologist who worked with Gray is testifying.
The defense called Dr. Kevin Richards to try and provide an explanation for Gray’s actions, as well as state if he can be rehabilitated enough to be eligible for parole in the future.
Richards said in court that he does not think Gray has schizophrenia, as he has suggested. He said Gray’s entire life was online, and he found a group there obsessed with school shooters.
“He was a lonely, dysfunctional kid who was anxious, paranoid, depressed and immersed in this highly dysfunctional world with these people obsessed with folks who’ve done school shootings,” he said.
The sentencing hearing began at 9 a.m. Barrow County Judge Nicholas Primm told Gray that he is facing a minimum of life in prison with possibility of parole and a maximum of life in prison without parole.
VICTIMS’ FAMILIES REQUEST MAXIUMUM SENTENCE
Families of those killed told the judge they prefer the maximum sentence. They delivered emotional victim impact statements after Gray pleaded guilty on Friday.
Breanna Schermerhorn, Mason’s mother, spoke first. She told the judge Gray knew the difference between right and wrong.
“I want it to be very clear that I do not forgive Mr. Gray,” said the mom. “The failures of the adults around him may explain parts of his story, but they do not excuse the decisions that he made. Those decisions were his and his alone, and because of those decisions, my Macy Mace is gone. My family, both biological and chosen, have been forced to endure horrors.”
Mason’s sister, Alanna Schermerhorn, took the stand next. She described entering college while trying to grieve the loss of Mason.
“I had to provide my brother’s death certificate to my school for my absences to be excused,” Allana explained.
Christian Angulo died while trying to shut the classroom door to save other students. His big brother, Junior Angulo told the judge to deliver the maximum sentence allowed by law.
“The defendant showed no mercy when he stole their futures. Therefore, he should not receive the grace of a second chance,” he said.
Coach Ricky Aspinwall’s wife Shana agreed.
“I ask that Ricky’s killer is not given an opportunity for parole. The trauma it would continue to bring me and my daughters knowing that there is a chance, even a small chance, that he would get out of prison would be continued torture for my family,” she told the judge.

Colt Gray Sentenced To Life Without Parole For The Apalachee High School Shooting At 16
Barrow County Superior Court Judge Nicholas Primm sentenced Colt Gray to life in prison without the possibility of parole on Tuesday, four counts of life without parole, one for each of the four people Gray killed at Apalachee High School in Winder, Georgia on September 4, 2024.
Gray, who was 14 at the time of the shooting and is now 16, pleaded guilty last Friday to all 55 counts against him including murder and aggravated assault. He did not speak at his sentencing.
"You do not seem to be tormented by what you did, you seem to relish following in the footsteps of the murderers you idolize," Judge Primm told Gray before handing down the sentence. "You aren't racked with guilt. You're proud of yourself. Your crimes reflect permanent incorrigibility."
The four killed were students Mason Schermerhorn and Christian Angulo, both 14, and teachers Richard Aspinwall, 39, and Cristina Irimie, 53. Nine others were wounded. Gray used an assault-style rifle he had received as a Christmas gift.
Prosecutors presented jail phone recordings during the sentencing hearing in which Gray appeared to relish the attention his actions brought him, including comparing himself to the man who attempted to assassinate Donald Trump.
His mother Marcee participated in calls with him and encouraged his growing notoriety. His father Colin Gray was convicted in March on charges of second-degree murder for providing the weapon.
The families of those killed were in the courtroom when the sentence was read.

sources.news_title: Apalachee High School Shooter Sentenced to LWOP, but What’s His Mom’s Deal?
sources.text:
I thought the sentencing for Apalachee High School shooter Colt Gray was going to happen yesterday. Instead we got another day of testimony rehashing stuff a lot of us already knew. He idolized other school shooters; he ran in those “true crime community” circles online, and despite what his own lawyers tried to sell early on, he wasn’t some psychotic kid hearing voices. He planned the shooting, and a notebook full of step-by-step notes doesn’t happen by accident.
The wait ended today, though. Judge Nicholas Primm sentenced Gray to life without parole. He looked the sixteen-year-old in the eye and told him he understood the horror he was going to do. Then Primm said that Gray was failed by his parents, failed by his extended family, and to some extent failed by society, but that none of that absolves him of who he chose to idolize, worship, and become. Gray cried in the courtroom hearing it. And you know what? The judge is right. Colt Gray was responsible. He pulled the trigger. Nobody else did that for him. But he was also failed, spectacularly, by the adults who were supposed to take care of him.
His dad’s failure is the one we’ve spent over a year talking about. Colin Gray put a rifle in his son’s hands, ignored every red flag law enforcement waved in his face, and is sitting in a cell right now because a jury decided that failure was criminal. Fine. We’ve covered that ground extensively, and on the 30th he gets his own sentencing hearing. The grandmother’s alleged failure, whatever it was supposed to be, I honestly can’t tell you. The record on that one is thin, and I’m not going to pretend I know something I don’t.
But Colt Gray’s mom. Holy shit, you guys. How did I miss this? Have we always known Marcee Gray was this far gone, or did I just gloss right over her because every camera in the room was pointed at dad? Because reading the transcripts of these jailhouse calls, I feel like I’ve been covering the wrong parent this whole time.
Let’s walk through what actually happened on these calls, because it’s worse than “supportive mom in denial.” This is a woman who spent months after her son murdered four people running his fan mail for him. He’d ask her to pull up what people were saying about him online, and she’d read it to him like a bedtime story. She’d allegedly bring him fan art comparing him to Adam Lanza, comparisons to Columbine, to Sandy Hook, and to the Aurora theater shooter.
At one point Gray asked her flat out if she’d made “the shrine” yet. Her response wasn’t horror. It was logistics. She needed to get some photos printed first, then she’d make the “Colty shrine.” Think about that for a second. A mother building a shrine to her son, the school shooter who killed four, and giving it a cutesy nickname like it’s a scrapbook project.
It doesn’t stop at passive enabling, either. When Gray wanted messages passed along to people he’d been talking to in his online communities before the shooting, she did it. She acted as his courier back into the exact online ecosystem that fed this thing in the first place. And when a journalist came sniffing around wanting to make a documentary about her son, Gray told her to go for it, and she apparently didn’t blink.
Investigators eventually got wind of these calls and cut her off with a no-contact order. Once that happened, staff say Gray genuinely changed. Not “seemed a little better.” Changed into what one official called essentially a different kid. That alone should tell you everything about how toxic that relationship actually was. And through all of it, when this finally caught up to her, Marcee’s defense was that she didn’t think they’d talked about anything inappropriate. Genuinely did not think it. That’s not a woman covering her tracks. That’s a woman who doesn’t understand what she did wrong, which might be even more concerning.
She might be the worst mother of a school shooter since Sue Klebold, and I don’t say that lightly. Klebold missed key factors in her son’s life that could have prevented Columbine. Marcee Gray was printing fan art to post on the fridge.
Wouldn’t it be the damnedest thing if it turns out mom wasn’t just tolerating his obsession with mass shooters but was actually part of that same online world herself, egging him toward it? We already know he was steeped in “true crime community” circles before he ever pulled a trigger. We know his mother had zero hesitation diving into that same content with him afterward, cheerfully, like she was in on the bit.
If there’s any chance she had a hand in shaping that fixation before September 4, 2024, instead of just cheering it on after, that’s not a footnote in a sentencing hearing. That’s a separate investigation, and it needs to happen. The dad’s locked up. The son’s locked up. Somebody explain to me why mom is walking around free.

sources.text:
Teenager sentenced in Georgia high school shooting that killed four people
WINDER, Ga. (AP & CBS) – A teenager who pleaded guilty to shooting and killing four people at a Georgia high school when he was 14 has been sentenced, while his father also awaits sentencing.
Colt Gray, who is now 16, was sentenced to serve life in prison without the possibility of parole. The judge called his crimes “deliberate, contemplated evil.”
Gray pleaded guilty last week to 55 counts, including murder, in the Sept. 4, 2024, shooting at Apalachee High School near Winder, about 45 miles northeast of Atlanta.
Barrow County Superior Court Judge Nicholas Primm handed down the sentence after hearing from family members of those killed and victims, as well as investigators, Gray’s grandmother and a forensic psychologist who had evaluated Gray.
Murder carries a mandatory sentence of life in prison in Georgia, so the only decision Barrow County Superior Court Judge Nicholas Primm had to make was whether Gray should ever be eligible for parole. He decided the teen should never be allowed out.
“You do not seem to be tormented by what you did. You seem to relish following in the footsteps of the murderers you idolize. You aren’t wracked with guilt. You’re proud of yourself,” Primm said.
“We’ve seen no evidence he has any ability to develop a conscience or any ability ever to fully value human life,” District Attorney Brad Smith had said during his closing argument, insisting that Gray “cannot be in society.”
Defense attorney W. Charlton Allen told the judge his client was “not irretrievably broken.” Allowing him the possibility of parole would give him “an opportunity of hope,” Allen said, adding that a lack of hope “takes away the ability for him to change.”
“This is not a happy day. This is a relief day, I would say,” Smith told reporters after the sentencing, adding that he hoped his team had “done honor” to the victims and their loved ones.
Teachers Richard “Ricky” Aspinwall, 39, and Cristina Irimie, 53, and students Mason Schermerhorn and Christian Angulo, both 14, died in the shooting. Another teacher and eight more students were wounded, seven of them hit by gunfire.
Victims of the shooting and family members of those killed conveyed their anger and grief to Primm, almost all of them asking him not to allow the possibility of parole.
Shayna Aspinwall, the wife of math teacher and football coach Richard Aspinwall, described “a life sentence of grief and trauma for those left behind.”
Investigators testified during the three-day sentencing hearing that Gray idolized mass shooters, talking about them online with other members of the “true crime community,” a group of young people online who are fascinated with such attacks. Gray had chatted online about gaining notoriety through a school shooting.
Prosecutors played recordings of phone conversations Gray had with his mother, Marcee Gray, from a youth detention center in the months after the shooting. During those calls, he directed his mother to look up what people were saying about him online. He was excited when she described “fan art” drawings depicting him or comments people made about him and the attention he was getting online.
Gray had the “mental wherewithal” to mimic details of other mass killings on the day of the shooting, Smith said. He placed those “Easter eggs,” anticipating that they would be mentioned in court one day and would perpetuate his fame, the prosecutor said.
“The shooting was not the culmination of the plan. The shooting was just one of the steps of the plan. The plan was ultimate and lifelong fame inside of the TCC,” Smith said, referencing the “true crime community.”
Gray’s grandmother says he needed help
“Colt got less stability than he needed, which made him even more vulnerable,” Allen, the defense attorney, argued. He said his client got wrapped up in an online community where he found the acceptance he craved but wasn’t getting at home.
Gray’s maternal grandmother, Debbie Polhamus, testified that the teen had a troubled childhood and that his parents failed him. Her grandson had grown “highly agitated and aggressive” in the weeks before the shooting, she said, adding that she had urged his parents to get him some help but they didn’t follow through.
“I tried to help Colt because nobody else was helping him,” she said.
Polhamus said she visits her grandson once a week at a youth detention center and that he has improved enormously with treatment and medication. She said her grandson has been doing a lot of reading and wants to study to get a GED diploma.
“I’d like to see him have a chance at some point to prove himself,” Polhamus said.
Gray was put in foster care while in detention because his father was in prison and there were concerns about his mother’s contact with him. Candice Broce, director of the state Division of Family & Children Services and commissioner of the Georgia Department of Human Services, managed his case.
Broce testified that Gray appeared to show improvement. After Marcee Gray was barred from speaking with her son by a July 2025 no-contact order and he started taking medication, staff at the youth detention center told Broce it “changed him essentially into a different child,” she said.
The judge acknowledged that Gray had been failed by his parents, his extended family and, to a certain extent, society.
“But that failure does not absolve you from who you chose to idolize, worship and become,” Primm told Gray.
Gray’s father awaits sentencing
Gray’s father, Colin Gray, is scheduled to be sentenced on Thursday after a jury convicted him earlier this year on 27 charges, including second-degree murder, involuntary manslaughter and cruelty to children. Prosecutors argued he provided the rifle used in the shooting despite repeated warning signs about his son’s deteriorating mental health.
